deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a reading excerpt, with paraphrase and short quotation, from Herbart's psychology of the categories (Ding/Substanz, Kraft, Ursache, Veränderung). It continues the previous page's notes on Hartenstein's edition of Herbart's works. That page is headed 'Hb. W. Bd. VII', which is in the hand of whoever transcribed it, not Riemann's. The page refs here (p. 273, S. 142 … p. 277, p. 280–283) plausibly point to Herbart's 'Psychologie als Wissenschaft', Part II, around §§144ff., but I am unsure of the exact volume and pages. The argument runs as follows.

(1) Herbart's realism has two sides. Idealism is refuted. Simple 'Reale' (einfache Wesen), originally free of any plurality of determinations, are posited, and every sensory property of a thing is reduced to the 'Zusammen' (co-presence) of such beings.

(2) The concept of Being 'wanders'. It retreats ever further behind sensory appearance, and the path from appearance to the Real that carries and explains it grows longer. Yet every stage of cognitive development must locate Being somewhere, or else everything would be represented as nothing. Where it is located characterizes that stage's world-view.

(3) p. 273, Substance. Common sense takes things (res, hence 'Realität') as the existent. Psychologically, things are complexions of characteristics (Complexionen von Merkmalen), and Being is ascribed to them directly. This is the 'first illusion': aggregates of sensory characteristics are taken as real unities without asking about the principle of their unity. Closer inspection finds only a manifold merely found together without a bond.

(4) The 'second illusion'. Through judgment, characteristics are detached one by one as predicates, the unities dissolve into predicates, and no subject remains. The subject's place is then filled by an unknown substrate (Locke is cited, 'S. 134'). This substrate is thought not as absolutely simple but either spatially (the atom) or as bearer of forces and activities (Leibniz's monads). That opens the way to manifold errors.

(5) One tries to drop the empty substrate and take the forces and activities themselves as the Real. This turns the Real into something relative and the absolutely posited into something conditioned, since activities need products and forces need a patient object. The notes then allude to causa sui and effectus sui.

(6) S. 142 … p. 277, Cause and effect in time. The common prejudice gives the cause temporal priority over the effect. Hume is cited as having remarked that if cause and effect were simultaneous, the temporal course of events could not be explained by causation. The notes then add that a cause which does not act at once leaves its effect undone as long as it postpones its action.

(7) p. 280–283, Change, force, cause. The changing thing is first grasped as a thing, i.e. a complexion of characteristics. Change means one characteristic leaves the complexion and an opposite one takes its place, while the persisting characteristics keep the thing 'the same'. The newly appearing characteristic is attributed to another thing as its property. Examples: lead as heavy and pressing down, fire as consuming, arsenic as poisonous. The names of the remaining examples are not legible to me. This yields the concept of a 'direction'/tendency in things, named 'force' insofar as it bears the new characteristics of other things; the cause is the thing that is supposed to contain the occurrence of the change.

(8) For natural-philosophical reflection, the indeterminacy in the concept of force (vis transiens) is more striking than in the concept of substance. The general natural-philosophical questions are set aside. The psychological ground of the prejudice that cause precedes effect is then explained: the new characteristic is referred back to a complexion that existed before. The next page continues with the example of a person who 'has long carried this guilt in her heart'.
errors: No mathematical derivations, so nothing can be checked for correctness. As a philosophical excerpt it faithfully reproduces Herbart's standard doctrine; no slips are detectable.

results.what: Excerpt and paraphrase of Herbart's psychological genesis of the categories of thing/substance (two 'illusions': aggregate-as-unity, then unknown substrate), and his critique of the substrate (atom, monad).
results.modern_name: Herbartian realism / psychological theory of categories

results.what: Discussion of the temporal priority of cause over effect, citing Hume, and a psychological explanation of the concepts of force and cause from change as the replacement of one characteristic in a complexion.
results.modern_name: Herbart's theory of causality and change (vis transiens)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart, drawing on Hume

deep.surprise_reason: These are Riemann's reading notes on Herbart. His intensive study of Herbart is well documented by his own statement in the published philosophical fragments, and the content is Herbart's, not Riemann's. There is no mathematics or original result.
transcription_corrections: Line 1 continues roughly: 'einfache Wesen, ursprünglich frei von aller Mehrheit von Bestimmungen, treten hervor; auf das Zusammen solcher Wesen wird jedes Merkmal eines sinnlichen Dinges zurückgeführt.'
'So wandelt der Begriff des Seins!' — Riemann underlines this phrase. A little further, 'vorgestellt würde' is more likely than 'wird'.
p. 273 paragraph reads roughly: 'Da nun der erste von den zuvor bemerkten Schritten bei allen Menschen wirklich vorkommt: so gelten dem gemeinen Verstande die Dinge für das Seiende…'.

The first-illusion sentence: 'Aggregate sinnlicher Merkmale, ohne Frage nach dem Princip ihrer Einheit, für wahre Einheiten … für real zu halten; während man … nicht einmal Dinge findet, sondern ein Vieles, das sich ohne alles Band bloss beisammen findet…'.

The second-illusion passage: '…die Stelle des Subjects, die gleichwohl der Prädicate wegen nicht wohl zu entbehren ist, wird ausgefüllt durch ein unbekanntes Substrat (wie bei Locke, S. 134), das gleichwohl nicht als schlechthin einfach (wie ein wahres Wesen) sondern entweder räumlich bestimmt (als ein Atom), oder als Inhaber von allerlei Kräften und Thätigkeiten…'.

The following passage includes: 'Dadurch verwandelt sich das Reale nun gar in ein Relatives, das schlechthin Gesetzte in ein Bedingtes; denn Thätigkeiten sind nicht ohne … Producte, und Kräfte nicht ohne leidendes Object' and later 'causa sui … effectus sui'.
The 'S. 142 … p. 277' passage mentions 'Hume' twice; it concerns a cause that does not act at once ('wirkt nicht auf einmal'), whose effect stays undone 'so lange … ihr Wirken aufschiebt'.

The p. 280–283 passage contains the examples 'das Blei als schwer und niederdrückend, das Feuer als verzehrend … das Arsenik als giftig wirkend' and the words 'Kräfte' and 'Ursache'. The word read as 'Richtung(en)' in several places may instead be 'Substanz'; the hand is ambiguous.
